title: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

hero.subtitle: The definitive requirements specification for Internet host software implementations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1122 defines the requirements for the software of Internet hosts on the communication protocol layers: link layer, IP layer, and transport layer. It is a cornerstone document that established the conventions for how Internet standards express requirements.

This RFC defines and uses the requirement words MUST, SHOULD and MAY (and their negatives), a convention later formalized in RFC 2119 and now standard language in Internet specifications.

MUST / MUST NOT
Absolute requirement. An implementation that does not satisfy a MUST requirement is non-conformant.
SHOULD / SHOULD NOT
Strong recommendation. There may be valid reasons to deviate, but the implications must be understood.
MAY
Truly optional. An implementation may include or omit this feature.
sections.eli5: Imagine a rulebook for a team game, with "you must", "you should" and "you may" written next to each rule. This rulebook is for the part of a computer that talks on the Internet.

sections.title: Link Layer
sections.content:
The link layer requirements cover how hosts interface with the physical network:

ARP Implementation
An ARP implementation MUST provide a mechanism to flush out-of-date cache entries (and, if that uses a timeout, the timeout SHOULD be configurable). It also MUST have a mechanism to prevent ARP flooding, meaning repeated requests for the same address at a high rate.
Trailer Encapsulation
Trailer encapsulation MAY be used only when both systems are known to support it. A system that does not negotiate it dynamically MUST have it disabled by default. The feature moved protocol headers after the data in Ethernet frames.
Maximum Transmission Unit
Ethernet has an MTU of 1500 bytes (1492 for IEEE 802.3).
sections.eli5: This is the first step: how a computer talks to its neighbors on the same wire. It has to learn neighbors' addresses and not use outdated notes forever.

sections.title: IP Layer
sections.content:
IP layer requirements cover addressing, routing, fragmentation, and ICMP handling:

ReassemblyMUST be able to reassemble datagrams of at least 576 bytes
TTLMUST NOT send a TTL of zero; MUST let the transport layer set the TTL, and a fixed TTL MUST be configurable
Source RouteMUST be able to originate source routes and act as the final destination of one; forwarding source-routed packets is a gateway function (§3.3.5)
ICMPEvery host MUST implement an ICMP Echo server function
BroadcastFour IP broadcast address forms are defined: limited, net-directed, subnet-directed and all-subnets-directed (§3.2.1.3)

The "Robustness Principle" (Postel's Law) is emphasized: "Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send." This principle has guided Internet protocol design for decades.
sections.eli5: This part is about addressed envelopes. A computer has to handle envelopes that arrive in pieces, not let them wander forever, and reply properly when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Transport Layer
sections.content:
Transport layer requirements cover both TCP and UDP:

TCP Requirements
A TCP MUST support urgent data, MUST implement Karn's algorithm and Jacobson's slow start. It SHOULD implement the Nagle algorithm, and SHOULD implement delayed ACKs (delay MUST be less than 0.5 seconds).
UDP Requirements
A host MUST implement the facility to generate and validate UDP checksums, checksumming MUST default to on, and UDP MUST silently discard a datagram with a non-zero invalid checksum.
Port Assignment
Well-known ports are used to access standard services (see Assigned Numbers).
TCP Feature
Requirement Level
Delayed ACKs
SHOULD (delay MUST be less than 0.5 seconds)
Nagle Algorithm
SHOULD implement, with a way for the application to disable it
Keep-Alive
MAY implement (MUST default to off; interval MUST default to no less than two hours)
Urgent Data
MUST implement
sections.eli5: Here are the rules for two kinds of conversations: a careful one where everything arrives in order (TCP) and a quick one where each message stands alone (UDP).

sections.title: Application Layer
sections.content:
While RFC 1122 focuses on communication layers, it includes guidance for how applications interact with the transport layer:

Interface Requirements
The host MUST provide a programming interface (API) that allows applications to: open/close connections, send/receive data, set TTL and TOS values, and be notified of errors.
Error Reporting
Transport and IP layer errors (ICMP messages, connection resets) SHOULD be reported to the application. The application should be able to handle these errors gracefully.
Multihoming
On a multihomed host, an application MUST be able to specify the IP source address for sending a UDP datagram, and for TCP the IP layer picks a local address if the application does not.

RFC 1122 is complemented by RFC 1123 (Host Requirements - Application and Support), which covers application-layer protocols such as Telnet, FTP, SMTP, and DNS.
sections.eli5: Programs need a way to ask the computer to open a conversation and to hear when something goes wrong. If a computer has several addresses, the program gets to pick which one to use.

references.text: Braden, R., "Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Application and Support", RFC 1123, October 1989.
Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", RFC 2119, March 1997.

subtitle: The definitive requirements specification for Internet host software implementations
summary: RFC 1122 states what an Internet host must, should and may do at the link, IP and transport layers, covering Ethernet and ARP behavior, IP handling and ICMP, and the details of TCP and UDP. It collects fixes and clarifications that implementers had learned the hard way, and is the companion to RFC 1123, which covers the application layer.

eli5.summary: This is a checklist for anyone building the part of a computer that talks on the Internet, saying what is a must, what is a good idea, and what is optional, so that all computers can get along.

tldr.problem: Different host implementations of the Internet protocols behaved differently, and the original specifications left many details open or ambiguous.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC goes layer by layer and marks each requirement as MUST, SHOULD or MAY (or their negatives), with explanations of the reasons and a summary checklist at the end.
tldr.outcome: It became the reference for correct host behavior and set the style of requirement levels used in later RFCs.

today: RFC 1122 is still the baseline for what TCP/IP hosts are expected to do, and later RFCs update parts of it. Its requirement words and its Robustness Principle (be liberal in what you accept, conservative in what you send) shaped how Internet specifications are written ever since. Some details, such as source routing, are now widely disabled for security reasons.
